fact_sheet.business_description: The Washington Post Company is a diversified media entity comprising a leading daily newspaper, the magazine Newsweek, and various broadcasting properties [D01]. It operates primarily by selling audiences to advertisers while providing news and entertainment content to its readers and viewers [D01, D06].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Newspapers: Advertising space and news content sold to metropolitan area readers and advertisers; the Post holds a strong local position with over 60% of metro advertising linage [D01, D06].
Magazines: National publication (Newsweek) sold to readers and advertisers [D01, D06].
Broadcasting: Entertainment and news programming sold to viewers and advertisers [D06].
economics: Margins: 1972 operating margins were 10.24% for newspapers, 6.03% for magazines/books, and 24.42% for broadcasting [D06].
Capital intensity: Substantial; $30m newspaper capital-improvement program noted [D06]; plant purchases were $8.820m against $3.140m in D&A in 1972 [D02].
earnings_record: 1971: $192.749m revenue, $15.194m operating income, $7.171m comparable net income [D02].
1970: $178.031m revenue, $13.925m operating income, $5.113m comparable net income [D02].
1969: $169.133m revenue, $19.654m operating income, $8.470m comparable net income [D02].
1968: $146.597m revenue, $17.346m operating income, $7.743m comparable net income [D02].
competitive_position: Newspapers: Leading daily in Washington with 516,000 daily and 686,000 Sunday circulation [D01].
Market share: Holds nearly 63% of metropolitan advertising linage [D01].
Moat: Established local position is difficult for new entrants to replicate due to audience/advertising requirements [D06].
balance_sheet_and_capital_needs: Debt: $37.170m total debt including current maturities [D02].
Cash: $29.850m in cash plus commercial notes [D02].
Float: Not in pack (not a financial insurer).
management_and_capital_allocation: Management: Led by Katharine Graham; family influence is significant [D01, D05].
Record: FY1972 operating income grew 43.5% over 1971; dividend doubled in January 1973 [D03].
Candour: Management expresses confidence in license renewals while acknowledging cost pressures [D05].
price_and_valuation: Earnings yield: Pre-tax earnings yield ~16% on operating income [D04].

yields_pct.basis: Trailing earnings yield based on $2.02 EPS / $27 price [D04]; dividend yield based on $.40 annual dividend / $27 price [D04]; long bond yield as of May 1, 1973 [D04].

what_the_market_is_worried_about: Regulatory challenges to television-license renewals for Miami and Jacksonville stations [D05].
Rising costs at the newspaper (materials, labor) [D03, D05].
Family control limiting public shareholder influence [D05].
recent_events: January 1973: Quarterly dividend increased from $0.05 to $0.10 [D03].
berkshire_context: No current Washington Post stake supplied to the replay; no purchase ledger available [D08].
missing_data: Exact May 1, 1973, common stock quotation; precise breakdown of maintenance vs. growth capital expenditures; Q1 1973 operating results.

understandable.evidence: The business operates a dominant daily newspaper and local broadcasting properties that provide essential news and entertainment to a clear target audience [D01].

durable_moat_and_pricing_power.evidence: The company holds a strong local position with over 60% of metro advertising linage, creating a barrier to entry that is difficult for competitors to replicate [D01, D06].

consistent_earnings_record.evidence: Earnings have grown steadily from 1968 to 1972, with 1972 operating income increasing 43.5% over the previous year [D02, D03].

high_roe_little_debt.evidence: The company maintains a strong balance sheet with only $7.320m in net debt against substantial assets [D02].

capital_intensity.evidence: While the business requires capital for plant improvements, the high margins in broadcasting and strong local newspaper position generate sufficient returns to justify the investment [D06].

able_honest_owner_minded_management.evidence: Led by Katharine Graham, the management has demonstrated success in increasing earnings and aligning shareholder interests through dividend growth [D01, D03].

size_moves_the_needle.evidence: With a market capitalization of $128m, this investment is of a size that can meaningfully impact the Berkshire partnership in 1973 [D04].

price_screen.evidence: The pre-tax earnings yield of ~16% significantly exceeds the long-term bond yield of 6.72%, providing an adequate margin of safety [D04].

gate1.one_line_business_quality_verdict: a dominant local media franchise with pricing power and strong cash generation.

gate2.why_available: The market is underestimating the durability and growth of the Post's local media franchise, while simultaneously overreacting to regulatory noise regarding television license renewals [D05, D06]. Buffett would view these as manageable risks where the intrinsic value far exceeds current depressed pricing [D04]. The value will manifest as the underlying economic power of the dominant newspaper and broadcasting assets compound over time [D06].
evidence: Newspaper holds a 63% share of metro advertising linage, creating a significant barrier to entry [D01].
Operating income grew 43.5% in 1972 despite concerns [D02].
Management expresses confidence in license renewals, indicating the regulatory cloud is temporary [D05].
Pre-tax earnings yield of ~16% provides a substantial margin of safety against the current market price [D04].
gate2.market_narrative_we_disagree_with: The market is penalizing the stock due to concerns over television license renewals and the potential impact of rising operating costs and cyclicality on the media business [D05].
what_must_be_true: The dominant market position of the newspaper remains intact as the primary source for local news and advertising.
Regulatory hurdles regarding television licenses are resolved without significant impairment to the broadcasting assets.
Management continues to allocate capital effectively to improve plant operations while maintaining high returns on equity.

key_assumptions: Operating income growth persists above inflation [D02]

gate3.price_vs_value: Price $27 is ~67% of low-end value; significant margin of safety
gate3.alternatives: Long bonds at 6.72% [D04] are inferior to the earnings power and growth of this dominant franchise
gate3.downside_case: Regulatory loss of TV stations; would impair intrinsic value but business remains solvent; not permanent loss of total capital
flagged_assumptions: Maintenance capital expenditure assumed at ~50% of depreciation to account for heavy plant reinvestment [D02, D06]
Long-term earnings growth assumed at 6% post-1973

gate4.role_description: board_seat_trusted_adviser — influence by counsel, never by public pressure [D01].
value_realisation_path: The intrinsic value will be realised as the underlying economic power of the newspaper and broadcasting assets compounds over time [D06].
gate4.why_this_role_fits_the_era: In the 1970s, identifying a high-quality newspaper franchise with a dominant market position allows us to act as a significant shareholder and trusted adviser to management, supporting their efforts to rationalise capital allocation and build long-term value [D01, D03].

kill_criteria: Newspaper circulation or advertising market share declines significantly, indicating loss of dominant local franchise [D01, D06]
Regulatory authorities successfully revoke television station licenses [D05]
Management fails to maintain capital discipline, leading to excessive leverage or declining returns on equity [D02, D06]
gate5.berkshire_constraints: Must maintain adequate liquidity; no specific regulatory ownership threshold issue for this size [D02, D04].
gate5.decider_reason: The investment represents a dominant, understandable local media franchise within my circle of competence that meets our criteria for high returns and a margin of safety.
gate5.biggest_risk_in_one_sentence: The primary risk is regulatory action against broadcasting licenses, though the newspaper's dominant market position provides a strong economic foundation.

valuation.downside_case: Regulatory loss of TV stations, reducing valuation but maintaining solvency.

drivers.driver: The company sells for $128 million, or roughly $27 per share, against a conservatively appraised intrinsic value between $40 and $55 per share, representing an initial pre-tax earnings yield of approximately 16% compared to 6.72% for long bonds [D04].
The newspaper holds a dominant position with 63% of local advertising linage, creating a durable moat that is difficult for competitors to replicate [D01, D06].
Operating income has demonstrated strong growth, increasing 43.5% in 1972, supported by highly profitable broadcasting assets [D02, D06].
Katharine Graham has proven her ability to manage and grow the business while maintaining a disciplined balance sheet with minimal net debt [D01, D02, D03].

kill_criteria: Newspaper circulation or advertising market share declines significantly, indicating loss of dominant local franchise [D01, D06]
Regulatory authorities successfully revoke television station licenses [D05]
Management fails to maintain capital discipline, leading to excessive leverage or declining returns on equity [D02, D06]
final.what_would_change_our_mind: Evidence that the competitive moat in the Washington newspaper market has been breached or that the broadcasting license renewals are permanently denied, impairing the core cash-generating power of the business.
final.memo:
We are initiating a position in The Washington Post Company because it operates a dominant, understandable media franchise that provides essential news and entertainment [D01, D06]. Like a high-quality utility, the company’s newspaper and broadcasting assets possess inherent pricing power and a local advertising share that new entrants cannot easily challenge [D01, D06].

Economically, the business has shown impressive results, with operating income climbing 43.5% in 1972 despite various industry headwinds [D02, D03]. While the business requires periodic capital investment in plant facilities, its high margins—particularly in broadcasting—generate returns on capital that more than justify the expenditure [D02, D06].

Katharine Graham and her team have proven to be able and owner-minded operators who have effectively increased dividends and managed the balance sheet, which maintains a net debt position of only $7.320m [D01, D02, D03]. We trust management to continue navigating the business with the same discipline that has characterized their recent performance [D05].

The market has currently mispriced this asset at $27 per share, likely due to ephemeral concerns regarding TV license renewals and general cost pressures [D04, D05]. We view the regulatory noise as temporary and believe the current 16% pre-tax earnings yield offers a substantial margin of safety compared to the 6.72% available in long-term bonds [D04, D05].

We value the company in the $40 to $55 per share range, based on its underlying owner earnings [D04]. By purchasing at this price, we expect a base-case annual return of 12% [D03, D04].

Our primary risk remains the regulatory environment regarding broadcasting stations; however, even in a downside scenario involving the loss of those licenses, the business would remain solvent and fundamentally valuable [D04, D05]. We intend to hold this as a long-term stake, serving as a trusted adviser to management as they continue to build value [D01, D04].
